entries.topicDescription: Reusing behavior with the 'by' keyword for properties and interfaces.

tips.title: Delegates.observable gives reactive state without a full Flow setup
tips.content:
For simple cases where you just need to react to a property changing —
logging, triggering a UI redraw, notifying a single listener — wiring up
a full StateFlow with collectors can be more machinery than the situation
needs.

Delegates.observable takes a lambda called after every assignment with
the old and new values, giving you lightweight change notification
directly on a plain property, without introducing a coroutine-based
reactive stream for a case that doesn't need one.

tips.title: lazy's thread-safety mode is configurable — don't pay for synchronization you don't need
tips.content:
by lazy defaults to LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED, which uses a lock
to guarantee the initializer runs exactly once even under concurrent
access from multiple threads — necessary for shared singletons, but pure
overhead in single-threaded contexts like a ViewModel property only ever
accessed from the main thread.

LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE skips synchronization entirely for a small
performance gain when you can guarantee single-threaded access;
PUBLICATION allows the initializer to run more than once under a race but
guarantees all threads see the same final value, trading a possible
redundant computation for no locking overhead.

tips.title: Delegated properties can back lazy, per-row data loading (e.g. a database cursor)
tips.content:
Loading every column of a database row eagerly, even ones a particular
query result never actually reads, wastes work when rows have many
columns but callers typically only touch a few.

A custom ReadOnlyProperty delegate backed by a Cursor (or similar lazy
data source) can defer reading each column until the corresponding
property is actually accessed, turning eager full-row materialization
into per-property lazy loading transparently.

tips.title: Class delegation works cleanly with generic interfaces too
tips.content:
It's easy to assume `by` delegation only works for simple, non-generic
interfaces — but a generic interface delegates just as naturally, with
the delegating class either fixing the type parameter concretely or
remaining generic itself and forwarding the type parameter through.

This pattern is common for decorator-style wrappers around generic
collections or repositories, where you want to add cross-cutting behavior
(logging, caching) without losing the generic flexibility of the
underlying interface.

tips.title: A delegate class's own equals/hashCode can leak confusing identity semantics
tips.content:
If a custom property delegate class doesn't override equals/hashCode, two
separately-created delegate instances wrapping the exact same underlying
value are still considered different objects — this matters if delegate
instances themselves ever get compared, stored in a Set, or used as map
keys somewhere in the codebase.

When a delegate class is meant to represent a value (not an identity),
giving it proper equals/hashCode (or making it a data class) avoids
subtle bugs where two logically-equal delegates behave as distinct
objects in collection-based code.

tips.title: Kotlin's delegation is resolved statically at compile time, not via a dynamic proxy
tips.content:
Delegation in Java is often implemented with a runtime dynamic proxy
(java.lang.reflect.Proxy) that intercepts calls reflectively — Kotlin's
`by` keyword instead generates real forwarding method bytecode at compile
time for every interface member, with no reflection or proxy object
involved at all.

This means Kotlin class delegation has effectively zero runtime overhead
compared to writing the forwarding methods by hand, and it's fully visible
to static analysis and obfuscation tools like DexGuard — unlike a
reflection-based proxy, which often requires explicit keep rules to avoid
breaking under obfuscation.

tips.title: Conflicting delegated interface members must be resolved explicitly
tips.content:
When a class delegates two interfaces to two different objects and both
interfaces declare a member with the same signature, the compiler can't
decide which delegate's implementation to use — this is a compile error,
not a silent pick-one resolution.

You must override the conflicting member explicitly in the delegating
class and decide manually which delegate to forward to (or combine both),
making the ambiguity resolution visible in code rather than hidden behind
an implicit rule.

tips.title: A ThreadLocal-backed delegate gives each thread its own property value
tips.content:
A regular property is shared state across every thread that touches the
instance — for genuinely per-thread values (a per-thread request context,
a non-thread-safe formatter reused per thread for performance), that
sharing is exactly the problem, not the solution.

A custom delegate backed by java.lang.ThreadLocal makes each thread see
its own independent value for the same property, with no cross-thread
interference — useful sparingly, since ThreadLocal usage on Android's
fixed thread pools needs careful cleanup to avoid leaking values into a
reused pooled thread.

tips.title: Default to val over var — pick mutability deliberately, not by habit
tips.content:
A val can only be assigned once (though the object it points to can still
be internally mutable, like a val pointing to a MutableList). A var can be
reassigned freely, which makes it harder to reason about a value's state
over a function or class's lifetime.

Starting with val and only switching to var when reassignment is genuinely
needed keeps more of your code provably stable, and often surfaces design
issues early — if you find yourself reaching for var frequently, it's
worth asking whether the logic could be restructured around immutable
values instead.
tips.codeSnippet:
val userName = "Ahmed" // cannot be reassigned
var retryCount = 0      // intentionally mutable — will change during retries
retryCount++

tips.title: The backing field is implicit unless you refer to it with 'field'
tips.content:
Every non-abstract property automatically gets a hidden backing field to
store its value, unless the getter/setter you write doesn't need one (for
example, a computed property that derives its value from other
properties).

Inside a custom getter or setter, the keyword `field` refers specifically
to that backing storage — writing `this.propertyName = value` inside the
property's own setter would call the setter again recursively and cause a
StackOverflowError, which is exactly why `field` exists as a distinct
reference.

tips.title: lazy delegate defers expensive initialization until first access
tips.content:
Initializing an expensive object (a regex, a large lookup table, a network
client) in a property initializer runs that cost immediately at object
construction, even if the property is never used in a given code path.

by lazy defers computation until first access and caches the result — by
default it's thread-safe (SYNCHRONIZED mode), but you can pass
LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE for single-threaded contexts where the
synchronization overhead isn't needed.

tips.title: Delegated properties standardize get/set logic across a class
tips.content:
Repeating the same validation or notification logic in every property's
custom getter/setter is verbose and error-prone when the logic needs to
change in multiple places later.

Implementing ReadWriteProperty lets you package that get/set logic into one
reusable delegate class, applied to any property with the `by` keyword —
Observable and Vetoable from kotlin.properties are built-in examples of
this pattern.

tips.title: Class delegation (by) composes behavior without full inheritance
tips.content:
Extending a class just to reuse its implementation (rather than because
of a genuine is-a relationship) tightly couples you to that class's entire
public API and future changes.

`class B(a: A) : InterfaceX by a` forwards all InterfaceX calls to the
wrapped `a` instance automatically, letting you override only the specific
methods you need to change — favoring composition over inheritance with
zero forwarding boilerplate.

tips.title: Map-backed properties for dynamic, loosely-typed configuration
tips.content:
Kotlin lets you delegate a property directly to a Map, reading and writing
by the property's name as the map key — useful for dynamic configs, JSON-
like structures, or wrapping something like a Bundle or JSONObject.

Use this sparingly: it trades compile-time key safety (a typo'd property
name just returns null/throws at runtime, not a compile error) for
convenience, so prefer it only at boundaries dealing with genuinely dynamic
data.

tips.title: vetoable lets a delegate reject a property change before it applies
tips.content:
Sometimes a setter needs to conditionally reject an update rather than
just observe it after the fact — for example, refusing to decrease a
counter below its current value.

Delegates.vetoable takes a lambda returning Boolean; returning false blocks
the assignment entirely, leaving the old value in place, while Delegates
.observable (its sibling) always allows the change but notifies after.
tips.codeSnippet:
var maxRetries: Int by Delegates.vetoable(3) { _, old, new ->
    new >= old // only allow increasing the retry count
}

maxRetries = 5 // applied
maxRetries = 2 // rejected — stays at 5

tips.title: provideDelegate customizes delegate creation per property
tips.content:
A normal property delegate is a single shared instance, but sometimes each
property needs a delegate configured differently based on the property's
own name or annotations — like a per-property SharedPreferences key.

Implementing operator fun provideDelegate lets a delegate factory inspect
the KProperty at declaration time and return a customized delegate
instance, commonly used to auto-derive a storage key from the property
name instead of hardcoding it.

tips.title: lazy — compute once, use forever
tips.content:
'by lazy' creates a property that's computed on first access
and then cached. The initializer lambda runs only once.

By default, lazy is thread-safe (SYNCHRONIZED mode).
Use LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE if you're sure it's single-threaded
for a small performance boost.

Great for expensive computations, dependency initialization,
or anything you want to defer until it's actually needed.

tips.title: observable & vetoable delegates
tips.content:
Delegates.observable() calls a handler AFTER a property changes.
Delegates.vetoable() calls a handler BEFORE and can reject the change.

Observable is great for logging, UI updates, or reacting to state changes.
Vetoable is perfect for validation — prevent invalid values from being set.

Both receive the property metadata, old value, and new value as parameters.

tips.title: Interface delegation with 'by'
tips.content:
Kotlin supports the Delegation pattern natively with the 'by' keyword.
Instead of implementing an interface manually, you delegate to another object.

This is a powerful alternative to inheritance. Your class gets all the methods
of the delegate, and you can selectively override specific ones.

Composition over inheritance, made trivially easy by the language.

tips.title: Delegate a property directly to another property with var x by ::y
tips.content:
Sometimes a property is meant to be a pure alias for another property —
keeping them manually in sync with a custom getter/setter that just
forwards reads and writes is boilerplate for something conceptually
simple.

`var alias by ::original` delegates directly to another property's own
backing storage via a property reference, so reads and writes to alias
genuinely read and write the original property, with no separate storage
or manual forwarding logic needed.

tips.title: A class can delegate multiple interfaces to different objects at once
tips.content:
Class delegation with `by` isn't limited to a single interface — a class
implementing several interfaces can delegate each one to a different
backing object, composing behavior from multiple independent sources
without inheriting from any of them.

This is useful for combining otherwise-unrelated capabilities (logging,
caching, networking) into one facade-like class, where each capability's
implementation genuinely lives in a separate, independently-testable
object.
